stem: A diploid cell with 2n = 8 chromosomes enters meiosis after S phase. How many chromosomes (each made of two sister chromatids) are in each cell at the end of meiosis I?

choices.choice_text: 8 chromosomes, each made of a single chromatid, because the cell divided like a mitotic cell
choices.rationale: Tempting if you treat meiosis I like mitosis. Mitosis keeps 2n and separates chromatids, but meiosis I separates homologs and halves the count. Fix: ask which structures are pulled apart.

choices.choice_text: 8 chromosomes, each made of two sister chromatids, because the cell has not yet divided its chromosome number
choices.rationale: Tempting if you think meiosis I only copies DNA. But meiosis I is a full division that halves the chromosome number. Fix: homologous pairs split in meiosis I, so each daughter cell has n.

choices.choice_text: 4 chromosomes, each still made of two sister chromatids
choices.rationale: Meiosis I separates homologs, so each cell receives one member of every pair (n = 4). The chromatids stay joined until meiosis II, which earns the point for tracking ploidy and chromatid structure.

choices.choice_text: 4 chromosomes, each made of a single chromatid, because the sister chromatids separated during meiosis I
choices.rationale: Tempting if you mix up the two divisions. But sister chromatids separate in meiosis II, not meiosis I. Fix: homologs apart first, sister chromatids apart second.

verification: Brief: homologs separate in meiosis I, sister chromatids in meiosis II. 2n=8 gives n=4 replicated chromosomes per cell after meiosis I.
author_flags: Seed asked mitosis vs meiosis comparison from observations; this item is a chromosome-count tracking question.

stem: A plant is heterozygous for two genes located on different chromosomes (AaBb). Which statement best explains why it can produce four genetically different types of gametes in roughly equal numbers?

choices.choice_text: Crossing over between the two different chromosomes swaps the A and B alleles into new combinations
choices.rationale: Tempting because crossing over also makes variation. But it swaps segments between homologs of the same chromosome pair, not between different chromosomes. Fix: independent assortment explains genes on separate chromosomes.

choices.choice_text: Mutations in each gene during meiosis create the new allele combinations in each gamete
choices.rationale: Tempting because mutation is a source of variation. But mutations are rare and create new alleles, not the regular four combinations of existing alleles. Fix: reshuffling of existing alleles is assortment.

choices.choice_text: The two sister chromatids of each chromosome carry different alleles, so they separate into different gametes during meiosis II
choices.rationale: Tempting because meiosis II separates chromatids. But sister chromatids are identical copies unless crossing over occurred. Fix: variation here comes from random orientation of homologs in meiosis I.

choices.choice_text: Homologous pairs orient at random in metaphase I, so the A/a and B/b alleles assort independently
choices.rationale: This is independent assortment: each homologous pair orients randomly, so every combination of alleles from different chromosomes is about equally likely. Naming the mechanism is what earns the point.

verification: Brief: independent assortment (random orientation of homologous pairs) gives variation for genes on different chromosomes; AaBb gives AB, Ab, aB, ab.

stem: In pea plants, tall (T) is dominant to short (t). A heterozygous tall plant is crossed with a short plant. What fraction of the offspring is expected to be short?

choices.choice_text: 1/2, because the Tt parent gives t in half its gametes and the tt parent gives only t
choices.rationale: Define the genotypes first: Tt x tt. Half of the offspring get T from the heterozygote (tall) and half get t (short), so 1/2 are short.

choices.choice_text: 3/4, because short is the phenotype shown by the parent with the more common genotype
choices.rationale: Tempting if you reuse the 3:1 ratio without checking the cross. Fix: 3/4 is a dominant-phenotype fraction for Tt x Tt, and this cross is a testcross giving 1:1.

choices.choice_text: 1/4, because a Punnett square always produces one homozygous recessive offspring in four
choices.rationale: Tempting if you remember the 3:1 ratio from a Tt x Tt cross. But this cross has a tt parent. Fix: write both parental genotypes before building the square.

choices.choice_text: 0, because the tall allele is dominant and masks the short allele in all offspring
choices.rationale: Tempting if you think dominance means the dominant phenotype always wins. But a Tt parent passes t to half of the gametes, and tt offspring appear when t pairs with t. Fix: dominance affects phenotype, not allele transmission.

verification: Tt x tt gives 1/2 Tt (tall) : 1/2 tt (short); Mendelian segregation per brief.

stem: In a species of beetle, a cross between a black-shelled male and a white-shelled female gives offspring that all have black-and-white speckled shells, with both pigments visible in separate patches on each beetle. Which inheritance pattern best explains the offspring?

choices.choice_text: Incomplete dominance, because the heterozygote shows a blend of the two parental phenotypes
choices.rationale: Tempting because both versions of the trait are involved. But incomplete dominance gives a new intermediate shade, not separate patches of each pigment. Fix: separate black and white patches mean both alleles are expressed.

choices.choice_text: Codominance, because both alleles are fully expressed in the heterozygote at the same time
choices.rationale: Both parental phenotypes appear side by side in the heterozygote, which is the signature of codominance. Choosing the model from the data pattern is the move that earns the point.

choices.choice_text: Complete dominance, because the black allele hides the white allele in the heterozygote
choices.rationale: Tempting if every trait is forced into a dominant-recessive model. But white patches are visible, so neither allele is hidden. Fix: check whether a parental phenotype disappears in the heterozygote.

choices.choice_text: Sex linkage, because the parents are of different sexes and the trait appears in all offspring
choices.rationale: Tempting because the cross used a male and a female. But sex linkage is shown by different results in male and female offspring, and here all offspring look alike. Fix: sex of the parents alone does not indicate linkage.

verification: Brief: choose the model from the data. Separate patches of both parental phenotypes = codominance.
author_flags: Seed was incomplete dominance in flowers; this item uses codominance with a different organism and scenario.

stem: Hydrangea plants with identical genotypes produce blue flowers in acidic soil and pink flowers in alkaline soil. Which explanation is most accurate?

choices.choice_text: Soil pH changes how the shared genotype is expressed, with no change in DNA sequence
choices.rationale: Phenotype comes from genotype interacting with environment. The identical genotypes show the plants carry the same DNA, so pH is shaping expression, which earns the point.

choices.choice_text: The plants in acidic soil must have a different genotype from those in alkaline soil
choices.rationale: Tempting if you assume every phenotype difference reflects a genotype difference. But the prompt states the genotypes are identical. Fix: when genotypes match, look to the environment.

choices.choice_text: The color difference cannot be inherited, so it has no connection to the genes of the plant
choices.rationale: Tempting because the environment clearly drives the change. But the genes set the range of possible colors, and the response to pH depends on them. Fix: genotype sets the potential and environment shifts the outcome.

choices.choice_text: Acidic soil causes a mutation that changes the flower color allele from pink to blue
choices.rationale: Tempting because the color changes with the environment. But the plants have identical genotypes, and soil pH does not rewrite a specific allele on demand. Fix: environment changes phenotype, not the DNA sequence.

verification: Brief: state genotype potential, then explain how environment shifts phenotype; not DNA change.

stem: A segment of one DNA strand reads 5'-ATGCCA-3'. Which sequence is the complementary strand?

choices.choice_text: 5'-TACGGT-3', because each base is replaced by its partner and written in the same left-to-right order
choices.rationale: Tempting because it pairs every base correctly. But the second strand runs antiparallel, so written 5' to 3' it is reversed. Fix: pair the bases, then reverse the direction.

choices.choice_text: 5'-ATGCCA-3', because both strands of DNA carry the same sequence
choices.rationale: Tempting if you think a double helix is two identical copies. But the strands are complementary, not identical. Fix: base pairing makes the second strand the mirror partner.

choices.choice_text: 5'-TGGCAT-3', because A pairs with T and G pairs with C, and the strands run antiparallel
choices.rationale: Complementary pairing gives 3'-TACGGT-5', which written 5' to 3' is TGGCAT. Using base pairing and antiparallel orientation together earns the point.

choices.choice_text: 5'-UACGGU-3', because the new strand is paired using uracil instead of thymine
choices.rationale: Tempting if you confuse DNA with RNA. But DNA uses thymine, and uracil only replaces it in RNA. Fix: A pairs with T in DNA.

verification: A-T, G-C pairing; 5'-ATGCCA-3' pairs with 3'-TACGGT-5' = 5'-TGGCAT-3'.

stem: After one round of semiconservative replication, how is a newly formed DNA double helix organized?

choices.choice_text: One strand is an original template and the other is newly made with complementary bases
choices.rationale: Each original strand guides construction of a new complementary strand, so every new helix is half old and half new. Explaining templating is the point earned.

choices.choice_text: Both strands are newly synthesized, and the original double helix stays intact elsewhere
choices.rationale: Tempting because it describes conservative replication, where the original stays together. But each parent strand is used as a template in the new helices. Fix: semiconservative means each helix keeps one old strand.

choices.choice_text: Both strands are the original strands, copied directly without new nucleotides
choices.rationale: Tempting if you think copying means moving the existing DNA. But new nucleotides must be added to build a second strand. Fix: replication adds new complementary nucleotides to each template.

choices.choice_text: Each strand is a patchwork of old and new fragments mixed along its length
choices.rationale: Tempting because Okazaki fragments make new DNA in pieces. But those fragments are joined into a new strand, not mixed into the old one. Fix: each strand is wholly old or wholly new.

verification: Semiconservative replication per brief: each original strand templates a complementary new strand.

stem: A eukaryotic gene has three exons separated by two introns. A researcher compares the primary transcript to the mRNA found in the cytoplasm. Which difference is expected?

choices.choice_text: The cytoplasmic mRNA keeps the introns, since they code for the amino acids of the protein
choices.rationale: Tempting if you think any long sequence is protein-coding. But introns are removed and exons carry the code. Fix: exons are expressed, introns are removed.

choices.choice_text: The cytoplasmic mRNA is longer because exons are added to the primary transcript
choices.rationale: Tempting if you think processing adds sequence. Processing removes introns and keeps exons. Fix: splicing shortens the transcript.

choices.choice_text: The cytoplasmic mRNA lacks the introns and has a 5' cap and poly-A tail
choices.rationale: Eukaryotic pre-mRNA is processed in the nucleus: introns are spliced out and a cap and tail are added before export. Knowing what processing changes earns the point.

choices.choice_text: The cytoplasmic mRNA is a DNA copy made by translation of the primary transcript
choices.rationale: Tempting because it confuses the two steps. Transcription makes RNA from DNA, and translation builds protein from mRNA. Fix: the cytoplasmic mRNA is processed RNA, not DNA.

verification: Brief: pre-mRNA is processed (splicing, cap, tail) before translation; introns removed.
author_flags: Seed was about alternative splicing and proteome size; this item is about basic processing.

stem: A DNA template strand reads 3'-TACGGA-5'. The mRNA made from it is read from its 5' end. What is the sequence of the mRNA?

choices.choice_text: 5'-TACGGA-3', because the codons are read directly from the DNA template
choices.rationale: Tempting because it is the sequence in front of you. But codons are on the mRNA, which is complementary to the template. Fix: transcribe first, then read codons.

choices.choice_text: 5'-AUGCCU-3', because mRNA is complementary and uses uracil instead of thymine
choices.rationale: Transcription pairs A with U, T with A, C with G and G with C, and the mRNA 5' end pairs with the template 3' end. This gives 5'-AUGCCU-3', so the codons are AUG then CCU.

choices.choice_text: 5'-UCCGUA-3', because the mRNA is written in the same direction as the template
choices.rationale: Tempting because it is the correct pairing written the wrong way round. But the strands are antiparallel, so the mRNA 5' end pairs with the template 3' end. Fix: after pairing, check which end is 5'.

choices.choice_text: 5'-ATGCCT-3', because the mRNA is complementary but keeps thymine
choices.rationale: Tempting because it gets the pairing right. But RNA uses uracil in place of thymine. Fix: replace T with U in RNA.

verification: Template 3'-TACGGA-5' -> mRNA 5'-AUGCCU-3' (pair, T to U, antiparallel): AUG start codon followed by CCU.

stem: In bacteria, the lac operon is transcribed only when lactose is present and glucose is low. A mutation in the gene for the lac repressor prevents the repressor from binding to the operator. What effect is expected when lactose is absent?

choices.choice_text: The operon genes are transcribed continuously, because nothing blocks the operator
choices.rationale: The repressor normally blocks transcription when lactose is absent. If it cannot bind the operator, regulation at the transcription step is lost and the genes are expressed constitutively.

choices.choice_text: The operon is transcribed only when lactose is present, because lactose still controls the operator
choices.rationale: Tempting because the normal system responds to lactose. But lactose acts through the repressor, which cannot bind here. Fix: if the repressor is nonfunctional, lactose no longer matters.

choices.choice_text: The operon is never transcribed, because the repressor is required to start transcription
choices.rationale: Tempting if you think a repressor is an activator. But the repressor blocks transcription. Fix: no binding means no block.

choices.choice_text: The mRNA is made but translation is blocked, because the repressor acts at the ribosome
choices.rationale: Tempting if you aren't sure where the control happens. But the repressor acts at the operator, controlling transcription. Fix: identify the regulatory step first.

verification: Brief: identify the level of regulation. Lac repressor acts at the operator to block transcription; loss of binding = constitutive expression.
author_flags: Seed was a eukaryotic enhancer experiment; this item is a bacterial operon with different logic. Glucose/CAP effect not tested.

stem: A researcher finds that a muscle cell and a neuron from the same person contain the same set of genes, but only the muscle cell makes large amounts of myosin. What best explains this?

choices.choice_text: The neuron lost the gene for myosin during differentiation
choices.rationale: Tempting because the neuron has no myosin. But the prompt says the genes are the same in both cells. Fix: absence of a protein does not mean absence of its gene.

choices.choice_text: Different genes are transcribed in each cell type, so they make different proteins
choices.rationale: Specialization comes from differential gene expression: the same genome is read differently, which gives different proteins and functions. The connection from expression to protein to function earns the point.

choices.choice_text: The two cell types have different DNA sequences because they came from different tissues
choices.rationale: Tempting because the cells look so different. But cells in one body come from a single zygote and share a genome. Fix: specialization reflects which genes are expressed.

choices.choice_text: The muscle cell has extra copies of the myosin gene that the neuron lacks
choices.rationale: Tempting if you assume more product means more copies. But both cells have the same genome, and gene expression levels are regulated. Fix: look at transcription, not DNA content.

verification: Brief: same genome, different expression; link expression pattern to protein set to function.

stem: The mRNA codon CAG codes for glutamine. A single-nucleotide change in the gene makes the codon UAG, which is a stop codon. What is the most likely effect on the protein?

choices.choice_text: A longer protein, because the ribosome reads through the mutated codon
choices.rationale: Tempting if you think a changed codon makes the ribosome continue. But a stop codon causes the ribosome to release the polypeptide. Fix: stop codons shorten, not extend.

choices.choice_text: A protein with the same length but one amino acid changed to a different residue
choices.rationale: Tempting because many point mutations are substitutions. But a stop codon ends translation rather than adding another amino acid. Fix: check whether the new codon codes for an amino acid at all.

choices.choice_text: No change in the protein, because the mutation is silent
choices.rationale: Tempting because only one base changed. A silent change still codes for the same amino acid, which is not the case for a stop codon. Fix: compare what the old and new codons specify.

choices.choice_text: A shortened polypeptide, because translation ends early at the new stop codon
choices.rationale: Follow the chain: DNA change -> codon becomes a stop -> translation ends early -> a truncated protein that probably does not work. Tracing the downstream effect earns the point.

verification: CAG (Gln) -> UAG (stop) = nonsense mutation giving a truncated polypeptide.

stem: Researchers cut a plasmid and a human gene with the same restriction enzyme, mix the fragments with DNA ligase, and insert the product into bacteria. What is the main purpose of the DNA ligase?

choices.choice_text: It cuts the DNA at specific recognition sites so the gene can be removed
choices.rationale: Tempting because enzymes in this procedure involve cutting. But cutting is the job of the restriction enzyme. Fix: restriction enzymes cut and ligase joins.

choices.choice_text: It separates the DNA fragments by size so the recombinant plasmid can be identified
choices.rationale: Tempting because fragments are often analyzed after cutting. But separating by size is gel electrophoresis. Fix: ligase connects fragments and does not sort them.

choices.choice_text: It seals the sugar-phosphate backbone to join the gene and plasmid ends
choices.rationale: Restriction enzymes make complementary ends, and ligase seals the backbone to produce recombinant DNA. Stating the input, the output, and what the enzyme does earns the point.

choices.choice_text: It copies the human gene millions of times using primers
choices.rationale: Tempting because it is another common technique. But that describes PCR, which uses a DNA polymerase. Fix: ligase does not amplify.

verification: Standard recombinant DNA workflow in brief: restriction enzymes cut, ligase seals phosphodiester bonds.
author_flags: Seed was a PCR/primer mutation item; this item covers restriction enzymes and ligase.

stem: A population of soil bacteria is exposed to a new antibiotic. Most cells die, but a few survive because they carry a gene for an enzyme that breaks down the drug. After several generations, most of the bacteria in the population are resistant. Which statement best explains this change?

choices.choice_text: The bacteria sensed the antibiotic and mutated on purpose to become resistant
choices.rationale: Tempting if you think organisms change because they need to. But mutations occur randomly, and selection acts on variants that are already there. Fix: need does not create the variation.

choices.choice_text: Each bacterium gradually became resistant during its own lifetime by being exposed to the drug
choices.rationale: Tempting because it sounds like individual adaptation. But natural selection changes the makeup of a population, not individuals. Fix: the proportion of resistant cells rose through reproduction.

choices.choice_text: The antibiotic caused the resistance gene to appear in the surviving cells
choices.rationale: Tempting because resistance appeared after the drug. But the drug is the selective pressure and the resistant cells carried the gene beforehand. Fix: the environment selects, it does not create.

choices.choice_text: Resistant cells survived and reproduced more, so the resistance allele became more common
choices.rationale: The chain is variation -> differential survival and reproduction -> increased allele frequency. The variation already existed and heritably affected fitness, which earns the point.

verification: Brief: variation exists -> some variants improve fitness -> alleles become more common; no need-driven change.
author_flags: Seed was Hamilton's rule and altruism; this item uses antibiotic resistance and basic selection logic.

stem: In a population of rock pocket mice living on dark lava, light-colored fur is heritable and is seen more often by owls. Over many generations, the average fur color of the population becomes darker. Which type of selection is occurring?

choices.choice_text: Artificial selection, because the fur color of the population is being changed by a choosing agent
choices.rationale: Tempting because something is selecting the mice. But artificial selection means humans choose, and here owls impose predation. Fix: natural selection arises from environmental pressures.

choices.choice_text: Stabilizing selection, because the average fur color is favored and extremes are removed
choices.rationale: Tempting because the population becomes more uniform. But in stabilizing selection the mean stays the same and both extremes are selected against. Fix: here the mean changes.

choices.choice_text: Directional selection, because the favored extreme, dark fur, shifts the population mean
choices.rationale: Owls remove the light mice, so dark mice leave more offspring. When one extreme is favored, the whole distribution moves in that direction, which is directional selection.

choices.choice_text: Disruptive selection, because both light and dark extremes are favored over intermediate fur
choices.rationale: Tempting if you only notice that dark fur is favored. But disruptive selection favors both extremes, and here the light extreme is selected against. Fix: check whether one or both extremes are favored.

verification: Mean shifts toward one extreme = directional selection (CED selection types); predation by owls acts on heritable fur color.
author_flags: Seed was disruptive selection on beak sizes; this item is directional selection with a different organism and answer idea.

stem: Farmers noticed that some wild mustard plants had larger flower buds and began planting seeds only from those plants each year. After many generations the plants produced very large buds, as in broccoli. What explains the change?

choices.choice_text: Each plant grew larger buds because it received more nutrients from cultivated soil
choices.rationale: Tempting because good growing conditions can increase size. But that would affect individual plants and would not be passed to seeds. Fix: a heritable change needs allele frequencies to shift.

choices.choice_text: Humans chose heritable large-bud plants as parents, so those alleles became more common
choices.rationale: Artificial selection requires a trait that is inherited, a selecting agent (the farmers), and differential reproduction. Naming all three explains the population-level change.

choices.choice_text: Artificial selection is unnatural, so the change comes from a mutation made by farmers in the lab
choices.rationale: Tempting because artificial sounds like manufactured. But the process works on natural variation through breeding. Fix: the mechanism is differential reproduction.

choices.choice_text: The plants developed larger buds because the farmers wanted them, and the plants responded to care
choices.rationale: Tempting because human demand seems to cause the change. But desire does not alter traits, and only heritable differences passed to offspring change a population. Fix: look for the selected trait and who reproduced.

verification: Brief: name the selected trait, who selects it, and how reproduction changes the population (Brassica oleracea example conceptually).

stem: A population of 100 diploid beetles has 40 individuals with genotype BB, 40 with Bb, and 20 with bb. What is the frequency of the b allele?

choices.choice_text: 0.5, because the b allele and B allele are equally common in heterozygotes
choices.rationale: Tempting because Bb individuals carry one of each. But the other genotypes are not equal in number. Fix: B = 120/200 = 0.6 and b = 80/200 = 0.4.

choices.choice_text: 0.6, because 60 of the 100 beetles carry at least one b allele
choices.rationale: Tempting because 40 + 20 = 60 beetles carry b. But allele frequency counts alleles, and heterozygotes have only one b. Fix: divide b alleles by 200.

choices.choice_text: 0.4, because there are 80 b alleles among the 200 total alleles
choices.rationale: Count alleles, not individuals: 40 Bb carry one b each (40) and 20 bb carry two each (40), giving 80 of 200 alleles. Allele frequency is therefore 80/200 = 0.4.

choices.choice_text: 0.2, because 20 of the 100 beetles have the bb genotype
choices.rationale: Tempting because it is the bb genotype frequency. But genotype frequency is not allele frequency. Fix: count every b allele, including those in heterozygotes.

verification: b alleles = 40*1 + 20*2 = 80; total alleles = 200; q = 0.4. Distractors: 20/100 = 0.2 (genotype frequency); 60/100 = 0.6 (carriers); 0.5 (assumed equal).

stem: In a population assumed to be in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, 16% of individuals show a recessive trait. What percentage of the population are expected to be heterozygous carriers?

choices.choice_text: 24%, because carriers equal p times q
choices.rationale: Tempting if you forget the factor of 2 in 2pq. But a heterozygote can form two ways, Aa or aA, so both are counted. Fix: use 2pq.

choices.choice_text: 84%, because everyone without the recessive phenotype must be a carrier
choices.rationale: Tempting because 100% - 16% = 84%. But that group includes homozygous dominant individuals as well as carriers. Fix: subtract the 36% that are AA to get 48%.

choices.choice_text: 36%, because the dominant allele frequency squared gives the carrier frequency
choices.rationale: Tempting because 0.6 squared is 0.36. But that is p^2, the frequency of homozygous dominant individuals. Fix: carriers are 2pq.
The recessive phenotype frequency is q^2 = 0.16, so q = 0.4 and p = 0.6. Heterozygotes are 2pq = 2(0.6)(0.4) = 0.48.

stem: Whales have flipper bones whose arrangement matches the arm bones of humans, yet they use their limbs very differently. Which claim and reasoning does this evidence best support?

choices.choice_text: Whales and humans evolved flippers and arms independently, because the structures serve different functions
choices.rationale: Tempting because function differs. But similar structure with different function points to shared ancestry, while similar function with different structure suggests convergent evolution. Fix: compare structure, not just use.

choices.choice_text: Whales and humans share a common ancestor, because homologous bones were inherited and modified for new uses
choices.rationale: Homologous structures share the same underlying design even when function differs, which is evidence of descent with modification. Linking the evidence to the claim earns the point.

choices.choice_text: Whale flippers and human arms are analogous structures, because both are used for movement
choices.rationale: Tempting because both help the animal move. But analogous structures have similar function without shared ancestry, and these share a bone plan. Fix: shared design means homology.

choices.choice_text: The bones are similar only by coincidence, so they provide no evidence for relatedness
choices.rationale: Tempting if you think similarity is always superficial. But a matching bone arrangement across many species is unlikely by chance. Fix: homology is a major evidence type for common ancestry.

verification: Homologous structures = evidence of common ancestry with modification (CED).

stem: Percent identity of a protein sequence compared with humans is: chimpanzee 99%, mouse 85%, chicken 70%, yeast 40%. Which conclusion is best supported?

choices.choice_text: Humans share a more recent common ancestor with mice than with chickens
choices.rationale: More similar sequences generally mean fewer mutations have accumulated since the lineages split, so a more recent common ancestor. The molecular data tie directly to the claim about recency.

choices.choice_text: Yeast cannot share an ancestor with humans, because the sequences are less than 50% identical
choices.rationale: Tempting if you think a low match means no relationship. But all eukaryotes share distant ancestry, and the differences reflect a long time since divergence. Fix: low similarity means more distant, not unrelated.

choices.choice_text: Chickens are more closely related to humans than mice are, because they come from an older lineage
choices.rationale: Tempting if you think older means closer. But sequence similarity is lower in chickens, meaning an earlier divergence. Fix: higher similarity means a more recent ancestor.

choices.choice_text: Humans evolved from chimpanzees, because chimpanzees have the most similar sequence
choices.rationale: Tempting because 99% identity is so high. But high similarity shows a very recent shared ancestor, not that one living species gave rise to the other. Fix: humans and chimpanzees share a common ancestor.

verification: More sequence similarity = more recent common ancestor (CED molecular evidence).
author_flags: Numbers are illustrative; no external source cited.

stem: After a drought, a finch population's average beak depth increases over several generations because birds with deeper beaks can crack the tougher seeds that remain. Beak depth is heritable. Which statement is the best description of this change?

choices.choice_text: Each bird's beak grew deeper during its own life as it practiced cracking hard seeds, and this was passed on
choices.rationale: Tempting because use seems to build the trait. But changes acquired in life are not passed on through DNA. Fix: acclimation is not evolution.

choices.choice_text: Evolution occurred, because selection changed the frequency of alleles for beak depth in the population
choices.rationale: Evolution is a change in allele frequencies across generations. Drought-driven selection on a heritable trait is a force that shifts those frequencies.

choices.choice_text: Evolution did not occur, because the birds only needed to change to survive
choices.rationale: Tempting if you think evolution is driven by need. But need does not produce evolution, while selection on heritable traits does. Fix: look at allele frequencies, not intentions.

choices.choice_text: Evolution occurred only if a new species formed, so this is merely a temporary fluctuation
choices.rationale: Tempting because speciation feels like the real evidence. But evolution can be small changes in allele frequency without speciation. Fix: the heritable shift counts.

verification: Brief: name the force and tie to allele-frequency change; evolution continues (Grants' finches pattern).

stem: A phylogenetic tree is written in nested notation as (((W, X), Y), Z), where each pair of parentheses marks a branching node and W, X, Y, and Z are living species. Which statement about the tree is correct?

choices.choice_text: W and X share a more recent common ancestor with each other than either does with Y
choices.rationale: Read relatedness from nodes. The W-X node is the most recent branching point, so W and X are each other's closest relatives, and Y branches off earlier.

choices.choice_text: W and Y share the most recent common ancestor, because they are both nested inside the same parentheses as X
choices.rationale: Tempting because they are in the same large group. But W and X form a smaller clade that excludes Y. Fix: the more nested the node, the more recent the ancestor.

choices.choice_text: Y and Z are the closest relatives, because they are written next to each other at the tips
choices.rationale: Tempting because the labels are adjacent in the text. But closeness at the tips means nothing; only shared nodes matter. Fix: find the most recent common ancestor.

choices.choice_text: Species Z is the ancestor of the other three species, because it is written last in the notation
choices.rationale: Tempting if you read the order as a time sequence. But all four species are living tips, and Z is simply the earliest branch from the group. Fix: tips are not ancestors.

verification: Nested structure: W+X node is the most recent; then Y joins; then Z. Closest relatives are W and X.
author_flags: Seed asked about distinguishing shared derived traits; this item tests node reading from a text-notated tree. Tree given as Newick-style text instead of a figure; checker should confirm it is unambiguous.

stem: Two populations of fish were once connected in one lake. A drop in water level split the lake into two separate ponds for thousands of years. When the lake refilled, males from the two groups no longer court females of the other group, and any hybrids are sterile. Which statement best describes how these species formed?

choices.choice_text: The two populations adapted to the same environment, so they became different species through identical selection
choices.rationale: Tempting because adaptation is part of evolution. But the same selection pressures would make populations similar. Fix: isolation plus divergence is the mechanism.

choices.choice_text: Sterile hybrids form new species immediately whenever two populations meet again
choices.rationale: Tempting because hybrids sound like a new kind. But sterile hybrids cannot pass on genes and show that species are already isolated. Fix: sterility is evidence of existing reproductive isolation.

choices.choice_text: The fish chose to stop mating with each other, and that choice made them separate species
choices.rationale: Tempting because mating behavior differs now. But this is a result of divergence, not its cause. Fix: explain what separated the populations and how differences built up.

choices.choice_text: Geographic separation stopped gene flow, so the populations diverged and became reproductively isolated
choices.rationale: Speciation needs isolation and divergence. A physical barrier prevents gene flow, differences build up, and isolating barriers (behavioral and hybrid sterility) then keep the species separate.

verification: Allopatric speciation: geographic barrier -> no gene flow -> divergence -> prezygotic and postzygotic isolation.
author_flags: Seed contrasted allopatric and sympatric speciation; this item is a scenario on how isolation leads to divergence.

stem: A population of lizards contains individuals with different toe-pad sizes. Which process is the original source of the new alleles that make this variation possible?

choices.choice_text: Crossing over, which makes brand-new alleles within each gene in every generation
choices.rationale: Tempting because crossing over produces new combinations. But it recombines existing alleles, not new alleles. Fix: mutation makes alleles, recombination arranges them.

choices.choice_text: Mutation, which creates new alleles that sexual reproduction can then reshuffle
choices.rationale: Mutations are the ultimate source of new alleles. Crossing over and independent assortment recombine existing alleles, but they cannot create new ones.

choices.choice_text: Exercise, because lizards that climb more develop larger toe pads that are inherited
choices.rationale: Tempting because use seems to build structures. But changes acquired by use are not encoded in gametes. Fix: only heritable genetic changes add variation.

choices.choice_text: Natural selection, which produces the toe-pad variants that individuals need
choices.rationale: Tempting because selection is tied to traits and adaptations. But selection acts on variation that already exists; it does not generate it. Fix: the environment does not create needed mutations.

verification: Brief: variation arises from mutation (new alleles) and recombination (new combinations).

stem: In a lab simulation of early Earth, a mixture of water, methane, ammonia, and hydrogen was exposed to electrical sparks. After a week, the mixture contained amino acids. Which conclusion is best supported by this result?

choices.choice_text: Organic monomers could form from inorganic molecules under hypothesized early-Earth conditions
choices.rationale: The experiment tests a hypothesis about prebiotic conditions and shows a plausible way to make organic building blocks. It supports plausibility, which is the level of claim the evidence allows.

choices.choice_text: Complete cells were formed in the experiment, showing how the first organisms emerged
choices.rationale: Tempting if you think amino acids equal living cells. But only small organic molecules were detected. Fix: cells need more steps such as membranes, polymers, and heredity.

choices.choice_text: Because amino acids formed, RNA must have been the first genetic molecule, before proteins
choices.rationale: Tempting because it is another origin-of-life idea. But this data says nothing about RNA or genetic information. Fix: match the conclusion to what was measured.

choices.choice_text: The experiment proves that life began on Earth through lightning and chemical reactions
choices.rationale: Tempting because amino acids are central to life. But making monomers does not show how cells arose, and science speaks in evidence-based support. Fix: do not claim certainty.

verification: Brief: state the hypothesis and the supporting condition or evidence; Miller-Urey type experiment supports abiotic synthesis of monomers.
author_flags: Seed integrated three pieces of evidence about RNA; this item is a single-experiment hypothesis claim.

stem: As day length shortens in autumn, deciduous trees stop making chlorophyll and drop their leaves. Which explanation links the stimulus, the response, and its advantage?

choices.choice_text: Temperature is the only stimulus because trees cannot detect day length
choices.rationale: Tempting because cold weather arrives at the same time. But many plants sense day length with photoreceptors. Fix: use the stimulus the prompt gives.

choices.choice_text: Shorter days trigger leaf drop, which cuts water loss and energy cost when light is scarce
choices.rationale: A complete answer names the stimulus, the response, and the fitness benefit. Here the benefit is conserving water and energy when photosynthesis cannot pay for the leaves.

choices.choice_text: The response is that leaves turn red, and it has no effect on survival or reproduction
choices.rationale: Tempting because color change is visible. But the key response is stopping chlorophyll production and shedding leaves, which affects survival. Fix: always state the advantage.

choices.choice_text: Leaves fall because the trees are dying at the end of their life cycle each year
choices.rationale: Tempting because dropped leaves look like death. But the trees live on and regrow leaves in spring. Fix: this is a regulated response with an advantage.

verification: Brief: identify stimulus, response, and advantage; photoperiod-driven leaf abscission conserves resources.

stem: A lake's producers fix 40,000 kcal/m2/year of energy. Assuming a typical 10% transfer efficiency between trophic levels, approximately how much energy reaches the secondary consumers (the third trophic level)?

choices.choice_text: 40 kcal/m2/year, because the energy is reduced by 10% three times
choices.rationale: Tempting if you count the number of trophic levels instead of the transfers. But that is the energy at the fourth level. Fix: transfers = level number - 1.

choices.choice_text: 32,400 kcal/m2/year, because the 10% is subtracted at each of the two steps
choices.rationale: Tempting if you treat 10% as the amount lost. But about 10% is the amount passed on, and about 90% is lost as heat and waste. Fix: multiply by 0.1.

choices.choice_text: 400 kcal/m2/year, because 10% is passed on at each of the two transfers
choices.rationale: Producers to primary consumers is one 10% transfer (4,000), and primary to secondary consumers is a second (400). Count transfers, not trophic levels.

choices.choice_text: 4,000 kcal/m2/year, because only one transfer is applied
choices.rationale: Tempting if you count the third level as one step from producers. But secondary consumers are two transfers away. Fix: apply 10% twice.

author_flags: Seed used 10,000 kcal and asked about tertiary consumers; this item uses different numbers and trophic level.

stem: A population of deer on an island is growing as shown by these yearly counts: 20, 40, 80, 160, 320. Later counts hover around 500 for many years. Which statement best interprets the data?

choices.choice_text: The population grows exponentially at all times, so the plateau is a counting error
choices.rationale: Tempting because early data show clear doubling. But no population can grow exponentially forever without limiting resources. Fix: check whether growth continues.

choices.choice_text: The deer must be K-selected because their numbers increased quickly at the start
choices.rationale: Tempting because K-selected species live near carrying capacity. But rapid early growth reflects abundant resources, not a life history strategy. Fix: infer K from the plateau.

choices.choice_text: The population has a carrying capacity of 20 because that was the first count
choices.rationale: Tempting if you take the first value as the baseline. But carrying capacity is the stable maximum a habitat can support. Fix: look at the level where the counts stop rising.

choices.choice_text: Growth is exponential early, then levels off near a carrying capacity of about 500
choices.rationale: Doubling every year is exponential growth with unlimited resources. The plateau shows limiting factors, so the island's carrying capacity is near 500.

verification: Doubling 20->320 = exponential; plateau ~500 = carrying capacity (logistic model per brief).
author_flags: Seed was about K-selected life history traits; this item interprets growth data. Data given as a text list rather than a graph.

stem: Which of the following is a density-dependent limiting factor on a population?

choices.choice_text: A parasite that spreads more easily as individuals live closer together
choices.rationale: Disease spread increases as crowding rises, so its effect depends on population density. Density-dependent factors get stronger as the population gets more crowded.

choices.choice_text: A volcanic eruption that removes a large share of the population in one season
choices.rationale: Tempting because it greatly decreases population size. But it acts regardless of density. Fix: natural disasters are density-independent.

choices.choice_text: A late spring frost that kills the same fraction of individuals in sparse and crowded groups
choices.rationale: Tempting because the frost limits the population. But the same fraction dies at any density. Fix: ask whether crowding makes the factor stronger.

choices.choice_text: A hurricane that destroys part of the habitat regardless of how many individuals live there
choices.rationale: Tempting because a hurricane affects the population strongly. But its impact does not depend on the population's crowding. Fix: weather and disasters are density-independent.

verification: Brief: density-dependent factors strengthen with crowding (disease, competition, predation); weather/disasters are density-independent.

stem: Clownfish live among the stinging tentacles of sea anemones. The clownfish gain protection from predators, and the anemone gets cleaned by the fish and receives nutrients from fish waste. Which interaction does this describe?

choices.choice_text: Competition, because both species use the same space on the reef
choices.rationale: Tempting because they share a location. But competition harms both species through shared limited resources, and here both gain. Fix: look for benefit or harm, not just overlap.

choices.choice_text: Parasitism, because the clownfish live on the surface of the anemone
choices.rationale: Tempting because living close together can look like parasitism. But the anemone is not harmed. Fix: parasitism requires one species to be harmed.

choices.choice_text: Commensalism, because the clownfish benefit while the anemone is unaffected
choices.rationale: Tempting because the fish's benefit is obvious. But the anemone receives cleaning and nutrients, so it is not neutral. Fix: check the effect on each partner.

choices.choice_text: Mutualism, because both species benefit from the relationship
choices.rationale: Name the interaction by its effect on each participant. Both gain here (protection for the fish, cleaning and nutrients for the anemone), so it is mutualism.

verification: Effects: clownfish +, anemone + = mutualism (CED community interactions).
author_flags: Seed was a trophic cascade with sea otters; this item tests naming a symbiotic interaction.

stem: Two meadows have the same number of plant species. In meadow 1, the species are common and about equal in number, while in meadow 2, one species makes up 95% of the plants. After a disease strikes the dominant plant of each meadow, which prediction about the ecosystem is best supported?

choices.choice_text: Meadow 2 is more stable, because one dominant species is easier for the community to rely on
choices.rationale: Tempting because a dominant plant seems strong and reliable. But depending on one species makes the system vulnerable. Fix: higher diversity spreads risk.

choices.choice_text: Genetic diversity within the plant populations is the only factor affecting stability
choices.rationale: Tempting because genetic diversity can help populations survive disease. But the prompt contrasts species-level patterns. Fix: name which level of diversity the question refers to.

choices.choice_text: Meadow 1 is likely more stable, because other species can fill the roles of the one that is lost
choices.rationale: Species diversity includes evenness as well as richness. In meadow 1 many species share the ecosystem's functions, so the loss of one has a smaller effect.

choices.choice_text: Both meadows are equally stable, because they have the same number of species
choices.rationale: Tempting if you count species only. But species diversity also accounts for how evenly individuals are spread. Fix: compare abundance as well as richness.

verification: Brief: specify the level of diversity (species) and consequence; even communities buffer disturbances.
author_flags: Seed concerned tropical forest carbon sequestration; this item concerns community stability and evenness.

stem: A small freshwater lake receives heavy runoff from fertilized farm fields. Algae multiply rapidly, and later the dissolved oxygen drops sharply and fish die. Which sequence best traces the disruption?

choices.choice_text: The runoff lowers the temperature of the lake, so the fish die from the cold
choices.rationale: Tempting if you grab any environmental factor. But the prompt points to nutrient enrichment and oxygen loss. Fix: use the evidence to choose the mechanism.

choices.choice_text: Fertilizer directly poisons the fish, so the algae grow because there are fewer fish to eat them
choices.rationale: Tempting because dead fish appear to be the problem. But the fish die after oxygen falls, and the algae rise because of added nutrients. Fix: find the first affected component.

choices.choice_text: Algae release large amounts of oxygen at night, which makes the water toxic to fish
choices.rationale: Tempting because algae do affect oxygen. But algae use oxygen at night and decay consumes it, causing a decline rather than an excess. Fix: follow the oxygen change correctly.

choices.choice_text: Excess nutrients cause an algal bloom, then decomposers use up oxygen and fish suffocate
choices.rationale: Trace the first affected component and follow the consequences: nutrients increase producers, then decomposition uses oxygen, and low oxygen kills fish. This specific chain earns the point.

verification: Eutrophication chain: nutrient runoff -> algal bloom -> decomposition -> hypoxia -> fish die.
